name: Leaf Rust
symptoms: Orange-brown pustules on leaf surface
Yellowing (chlorosis) around pustules
Premature leaf drop and wilting
Reduced grain fill in severe cases
cause: Fungal pathogen Puccinia triticina, spreads in warm humid conditions (15–25°C). Wind-dispersed spores travel long distances.
treatment_steps: Apply propiconazole fungicide at 0.1% concentration immediately
Spray tebuconazole 250 EC at 1 ml/litre of water
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant material
Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness
prevention_tips: Use rust-resistant wheat varieties (HD-2967, PBW-343)
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
Apply balanced fertilizers — avoid excess nitrogen
Monitor fields regularly especially during humid spells

name: Powdery Mildew
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaf surface and stems
Yellowing and curling of infected leaves
Stunted plant growth
Premature defoliation in severe infections
cause: Fungal pathogen Blumeria graminis / Erysiphe species. Thrives in dry weather with high humidity — cool temperatures 15–22°C.
treatment_steps: Apply sulfur-based fungicide (wettable sulfur) at 3 g/litre
Spray hexaconazole or propiconazole at recommended rates
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
Improve air circulation between plants
prevention_tips: Plant mildew-resistant varieties
Avoid dense planting — maintain proper row spacing
Do not apply excess nitrogen fertilizer
Early season monitoring and preventive sprays

name: Rice Blast
symptoms: Diamond-shaped lesions with gray centers and brown borders on leaves
White to gray patches on flower neck (neck rot)
Lesions on leaf collars and internodes
Panicle collapse in neck blast stage
cause: Fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae. Favored by moderate temperatures (24–28°C), high humidity, and heavy dew.
treatment_steps: Apply tricyclazole at 0.6 g/litre or isoprothiolane at 1.5 ml/litre
Spray at tillering and panicle initiation stages
Avoid water stress — maintain proper field flooding
Drain water from nursery beds if blast appears
prevention_tips: Use blast-resistant rice varieties (IR-64, Swarna)
Apply balanced silicon fertilization
Avoid excessive nitrogen application
Use disease-free seeds and treat with fungicide before sowing

name: Early Blight
symptoms: Dark brown concentric ring spots on older leaves
Target-board appearance: alternating light and dark rings
Yellowing around lesions
Fruit lesions — dark, sunken spots with concentric rings
cause: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani. Spreads during warm temperatures (24–29°C) with frequent rain and high humidity.
treatment_steps: Apply mancozeb 75 WP at 2.5 g/litre as protective spray
Use chlorothalonil or copper oxychloride for systemic control
Remove infected lower leaves immediately
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation instead
prevention_tips: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Maintain proper spacing for air circulation
Crop rotation — avoid planting solanaceous crops consecutively
Apply mulch to prevent soil-splash spread

name: Late Blight
symptoms: Water-soaked greenish spots on leaf edges and tips
Spots turn dark brown/black rapidly in wet conditions
White fluffy fungal growth on underside of leaves
Tuber rot — brown decay with firm texture
cause: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Spreads rapidly in cool (10–20°C), wet conditions. Can destroy entire field in days.
treatment_steps: Apply metalaxyl + mancozeb combination at 2.5 g/litre immediately
Spray cymoxanil + famoxadone (Equation Pro) in severe cases
Remove and destroy infected plant material far from field
Improve field drainage to reduce waterlogging
prevention_tips: Use certified, blight-resistant potato varieties
Avoid planting in poorly drained fields
Begin preventive fungicide spray program before rains
Monitor weather forecasts — spray before high-risk periods

name: Fusarium Wilt
symptoms: One-sided yellowing and wilting of leaves
Brown discoloration of vascular tissue when stem is cut
Lower leaves drop first, progressing upward
Complete plant collapse in severe infection
cause: Soil-borne fungal pathogen Fusarium oxysporum. Enters through roots, spreads through vascular tissue. Persists in soil for years.
treatment_steps: Apply carbendazim 50 WP at 2 g/litre as soil drench
Remove and destroy infected plants with roots immediately
Drench soil with trichoderma-based biocontrol (5 g/litre)
Improve soil drainage — avoid waterlogging
prevention_tips: Use Fusarium-resistant varieties where available
Soil solarization before planting season
Long-term crop rotation (3–4 years) with non-host crops
Treat seeds with trichoderma before sowing

name: Downy Mildew
symptoms: Yellow patches on upper surface of leaves
Gray-purple downy fungal growth on leaf undersides
Leaf distortion and curling
Stunted growth and premature defoliation
cause: Oomycete pathogen Plasmopara / Peronospora species. Favored by cool temperatures (15–20°C) with high moisture and fog.
treatment_steps: Apply metalaxyl MZ (Ridomil Gold) at 2 g/litre
Spray copper oxychloride 50 WP at 3 g/litre as preventive
Remove infected leaves and improve air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in evening or morning
prevention_tips: Plant resistant varieties
Ensure good air movement in the field
Avoid irrigation late in the day — keep foliage dry overnight
Apply preventive copper-based fungicide at early growth stages

name: Anthracnose
symptoms: Sunken, dark brown to black lesions on fruits and leaves
Salmon-pink spore masses in moist conditions
Fruit rot with dark concentric rings
Stem cankers and shoot dieback
cause: Fungal pathogen Colletotrichum species. Spreads via rain splash and insects. Survives in infected debris and soil.
treatment_steps: Apply carbendazim 50 WP at 1 g/litre or mancozeb at 2.5 g/litre
Spray thiophanate-methyl for systemic control
Prune and destroy infected branches and fruit
Post-harvest treatment with hot water (52°C for 5 minutes) for fruits
prevention_tips: Use disease-free planting material
Avoid overhead irrigation during fruiting stage
Regular orchard sanitation — remove fallen fruit and debris
Preventive fungicide spray before rainy season

name: Bacterial Leaf Spot
symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown/black
Spots with yellow halos on leaf surface
Lesions may merge, causing large necrotic areas
Fruit spots — raised, scabby, white-to-brown lesions
cause: Bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas campestris / Pseudomonas syringae. Spreads via rain, insects, tools, and infected seeds.
treatment_steps: Apply copper-based bactericide (copper hydroxide) at 3 g/litre
Spray streptomycin sulfate at 200 ppm concentration
Remove infected plant material and sanitize tools
Reduce overhead irrigation and improve air circulation
prevention_tips: Use certified disease-free seeds
Treat seeds with hot water (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice crop rotation — avoid planting same crop family consecutively
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet

name: Root Rot
symptoms: Dark brown to black rotting of root tissue
Wilting and yellowing of entire plant despite adequate water
Plant pulls out easily from soil with decayed roots
Crown and stem base rot near soil line
cause: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium, Phytophthora) thriving in waterlogged or poorly drained soils.
treatment_steps: Seed treatment with thiram or captan at 2.5 g/kg seed
Soil drench with metalaxyl or carbendazim around root zone
Improve field drainage — create drainage channels
Remove and destroy severely affected plants
prevention_tips: Avoid waterlogging — proper land leveling and drainage
Treat seeds with biocontrol agents (Trichoderma viride)
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
Soil solarization in problem fields before planting

name: Mosaic Virus
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf puckering, curling, and distortion
Stunted plant growth and reduced fruit set
Mottled, misshapen fruits with reduced quality
cause: Caused by Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) and others. Spreads by aphids, thrips, and mechanical contact.
treatment_steps: No chemical cure — remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Control aphid vectors with imidacloprid at 0.5 ml/litre
Apply mineral oil spray to deter aphid feeding and virus spread
Wash hands and disinfect tools between plants with bleach solution
prevention_tips: Use virus-resistant or virus-tolerant varieties
Control aphid populations early in the season
Avoid handling plants from infected to healthy sections
Plant borders of taller crops to reduce aphid migration

name: Smut
symptoms: Black powdery masses replacing grain (loose smut in wheat)
Whip-like curved galls in sugarcane — black spore masses
Infected ears appear normal initially, then burst with black spores
Complete replacement of grain with black, sooty fungal material
cause: Fungal pathogens Ustilago species. Seed-borne and air-borne. Spores infect at seedling stage through soil and seed.
treatment_steps: Seed treatment with carboxin + thiram at 1.5 g/kg seed
Hot water seed treatment at 52°C for 10 minutes before sowing
Remove and destroy infected whip ear in sugarcane immediately
Apply systemic fungicide (triadimefon) at early symptom stage
prevention_tips: Use smut-free certified seeds
Seed treatment is the most effective prevention
Crop rotation with non-cereal crops
Avoid replanting ratoon crops in smut-affected sugarcane fields

name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
symptoms: Small circular to oval spots with gray/white centers
Dark brown to purple borders around spots
Spots may merge causing irregular brown blotches
Dark velvety sporulation on leaf undersides in humid conditions
cause: Fungal pathogen Cercospora species. Spreads in warm (25–30°C), humid conditions via air-borne conidia.
treatment_steps: Apply carbendazim 50 WP at 1 g/litre or chlorothalonil at 2 g/litre
Spray propiconazole for systemic control in severe cases
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves
Apply preventive sprays at canopy closure stage
prevention_tips: Use resistant varieties
Avoid dense planting and maintain row spacing for air circulation
Balanced fertilization — avoid excess nitrogen
Crop rotation with non-host crops

name: Iron Deficiency
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis — leaves turn yellow while veins stay green
Younger leaves affected first (top of plant)
In severe cases, leaves turn completely yellow/white
Stunted plant growth and reduced tillering
cause: Iron deficiency in calcareous or waterlogged soils with high pH (>7.5). Not enough available iron for chlorophyll production.
treatment_steps: Foliar spray of ferrous sulfate (FeSO4) at 5 g/litre every 7–10 days
Soil application of iron chelate (Fe-EDTA) at 5 kg/acre
Acidify soil around roots with sulfur application
Apply ferric ammonium citrate as foliar spray for quick response
prevention_tips: Soil testing before crop planting to check iron and pH levels
Use iron-efficient varieties for alkaline soils
Avoid waterlogging which increases soil pH
Incorporate organic matter to improve iron availability

name: Nitrogen Deficiency
symptoms: Pale yellow to light green coloration starting in older lower leaves
Yellowing progresses upward through the plant canopy
Thin, spindly stalks and reduced plant vigor
Premature leaf senescence and poor grain fill
cause: Insufficient nitrogen in soil due to low organic matter, leaching, or poor fertilizer management.
treatment_steps: Apply urea (46-0-0) at recommended rate based on crop and growth stage
Use split application — basal + top dressing at tillering
Foliar spray of urea at 2% concentration for quick green-up
Apply ammonium sulfate on alkaline soils for better nitrogen availability
prevention_tips: Soil test before each season to determine nitrogen requirement
Incorporate green manure and organic compost before planting
Use controlled-release nitrogen fertilizers to reduce leaching
Include legume crop in rotation to fix atmospheric nitrogen naturally
